Unawares
un-uh-WAIRZ
adv.
From unaware plus the adverbial -s. Webster 1828: unexpectedly; suddenly; without previous preparation; also, without design or intention. The Authorized Version uses it in both senses, and the difference between them decides two of the most important passages in the law and in the epistles.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Unawares in the KJV runs along two tracks. The first is the manslayer’s: the cities of refuge exist that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares (Numbers 35:11), and Joshua repeats it of the man who kills unawares and unwittingly (Joshua 20:3). Here the word means without intention, and the whole architecture of the six cities rests on the distinction between the murderer and the man whose axe head flew off. God’s law grades guilt by intent and provides a refuge for the one and none for the other. The second track is the church’s danger and it means undetected. Paul warns of false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus (Galatians 2:4), and Jude of certain men crept in unawares… turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness (Jude 4). Error does not usually arrive announced. The third use is the sweetest: Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2). And our Lord warns that the last day may come upon you unawares (Luke 21:34), which is why the same chapter commands watching.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines UNAWARES as unexpectedly; suddenly; at a time when not thought of; also, without design; inadvertently. The KJV uses the second sense of the manslayer and the first of the false teacher and the day of the Lord.

expand to see more

UNAWARES, adv. — Unexpectedly; suddenly; at a time when not thought of; without preparation.

Also, without design or intention; inadvertently; as, to injure a man unawares.

Webster’s two senses are exactly the two the Authorized Version employs, and confusing them ruins the law of the cities of refuge. To kill a man at unawares is not to be surprised by it; it is to have had no intention of it.

Key Scripture

Numbers 35:11 — "Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares."

Joshua 20:3 — "That the slayer that killeth any person unawares and unwittingly may flee thither: and they shall be your refuge from the avenger of blood."

Galatians 2:4 — "And that because of false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage:"

Hebrews 13:2 — "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares."

Luke 21:34 — "And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares."

Modern Corruption

The word is corrupted when the law’s careful distinction between intentional and unintentional bloodshed is flattened — in either direction — and when Galatians 2:4 and Jude 4 are treated as intemperance rather than as apostolic description of how error actually enters a church.

expand to see more

Numbers 35 is one of the clearest refutations of the claim that the Mosaic law is indiscriminate. Six cities are appointed, spread through the land, open to the Israelite and to the stranger alike (Numbers 35:15), for the man who killed unawares. The chapter then distinguishes him from the murderer by weapon, by motive, and by prior enmity, and requires a congregation to judge between them. Intent matters to God; so does bloodshed. A modern reading that treats the Old Testament as uniformly harsh has not read this chapter, and a reading that treats intention as the only thing that matters has not read the rest of it — the manslayer still had to flee, and still had to remain until the death of the high priest.

Galatians 2:4 and Jude 4 describe a mechanism, not a mood. False brethren are unawares brought in; ungodly men crept in unawares. Neither apostle imagines heresy arriving with a banner. It comes in through the ordinary doors of hospitality, friendship, and shared vocabulary, which is precisely why Jude and Paul both write to congregations that had not noticed. The remedy Scripture gives is not suspicion of strangers — Hebrews 13:2 forbids that in the same word — but a confessing, watchful eldership that knows what it holds. This is the practical case for a confession of faith: a church that has written down what it believes can tell when something has crept in.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew is bishgagah, in error or inadvertently, the standing legal term for unintentional sin; the Greek words in Galatians and Jude mean brought in alongside and slipped in beside.

expand to see more

Hebrew shegagah (H7684) — error, inadvertence; the legal category of unintentional sin and unintentional killing (Numbers 35:11; Joshua 20:3).

Hebrew bibli da'ath — without knowledge; the phrase Joshua 20:3 pairs with it, rendered unwittingly.

Greek pareisaktos (G3920) — brought in alongside, smuggled in; false brethren unawares brought in (Galatians 2:4).

Greek pareisduno (G3921) — to slip in beside, to creep in stealthily; crept in unawares (Jude 4).

Greek lanthano (G2990) — to escape notice; behind entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2).

Usage

"Which killeth any person at unawares (Numbers 35:11) — the legal category of unintentional bloodshed, for which God appointed refuge."

"False brethren unawares brought in (Galatians 2:4) — error enters undetected, through ordinary doors."

"Some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2) — the same adverb turned to blessing; hospitality without knowing what is being received."
